We've already seen numerous examples of why granting Meta's Muse app full disk access on Mac is an absolutely terrible idea, and now another major privacy issue has surfaced: Muse has been found to analyze your communications with everyone in your life every single hour.

Apple has responded to the development with understandable concern, stating in a blog post that it will be introducing additional controls for the 'Full Disk Access' feature that caused the issue in the first place…

Meta Muse app makes this urgent

Meta recently launched its Muse personal AI agent app for iPhone and Mac. Despite the obvious inadvisability of giving an unfettered Meta app access to everything on your Apple device, the app quickly rocketed to the top of the App Store charts.

Predictably, it wasn't long before serious problems started to surface, and things haven't gotten better since. Wired reports that security researcher Karan Joshi discovered Meta has instructed Muse to extract all the information needed to build a complete map of every one of the user's relationships.

One of Muse's instructions appears to be to create 'a page for every person in the user's life.' This hourly process, according to its instructions, collects data on family members, partners, friends, colleagues, 'collaborators,' and people the user 'tracks'… The instructions state: 'Where they live, what they do, recurring topics (the apartment move, the shared savings goal).' Instructions also add that the model can note 'significant days,' such as birthdays or anniversaries. A person's history can include contextual details like 'the March trip, the argument that was resolved, last week's milestone.'

Apple tightens Full Disk Access controls

You might think that the prompt explaining what granting an app Full Disk Access on Mac means is clear enough, but that doesn't seem to be the case. Even tech-savvy users have been handing over this all-access pass to their computers without realizing just how dangerous a step it is.

Apple says the feature was originally designed for backup apps, but developers have since found many more uses for it, including AI agents. The company has said it intends to 'introduce additional controls' to ensure users fully understand what they're doing when they grant this permission.

What Apple must and must not do

Apple says this step is 'essential,' and I entirely agree. When existing permission requests clearly fail to adequately convey the gravity of what is being granted, Apple must make sure users truly understand what they are allowing.

What I would like to see is clearer, more explicit text dissuading users from doing this unless they truly understand the consequences. Something roughly along the lines of:

Basically, the wording cannot be too strong. I'd also be happy to accept a one-time confirmation for apps that have already been granted this permission.

Popular comments from Peter

While I find it slightly annoying that Apple periodically asks me whether I want to continue allowing apps to access Location, I do appreciate it. There have been at least one or two occasions when I realized I didn't want an app to have that level of access anymore. It also serves as a reminder to regularly think about which apps might be using my location data.

However, Apple absolutely must not repeat the mistake it made with Screen Recording on macOS Sequoia. While this is equally extremely dangerous and warrants a very strong warning, what Apple did was force us to confirm these permissions every single week, and then again every time we rebooted.

This was widely criticized as turning macOS into Microsoft Vista and imposing a 'subscription you didn't buy and can't cancel.' In my view, Apple has already gone too far with occasional re-confirmation of permissions on iPhone. For example, I've granted Citymapper access to Location so it can keep providing navigation in the background, so Apple, I really don't need you to ask me again whether I still want this.

Yes, give the strongest possible warning about Full Disk Access, but if someone chooses to grant it, macOS must respect that decision. No more weekly or any kind of forced re-confirmations, thanks.
